name: Thermocap

lead: The Thermocap was a scalp cap sold in the 1920s by the Merke Institutes of New York. It was a bonnet with a socket at the top for a standard light bulb, and advertisements claimed hair roots were dormant rather than dead.

The idea was that warming the scalp with heat and light for about 15 minutes a day would relax and open the pores and revive thinning hair, giving a fuller head of hair. No published trials of the device are known.

paras: The user wore the cap with a bulb screwed in and sat under it daily for a short session. Ads promised new hair in 30 days or money back.
No clinical safety data on the device exist. It is mainly remembered today as an example of early-20th-century hair-loss gadgets.

angle.text: The Thermocap's maker claimed that a daily 15-minute session of heat and light would revive dormant follicles. It is a historical device, not a currently marketed product.

lead: The Thermocap was a hair-loss device associated with Aloise A. Merke, who was awarded a patent on 22 September 1925, originally assigned to the Thompson Barlow Company; it was later produced by Allied Merke Institutes, Inc. of New York [1].

It was described as a cap with a socket at the top into which a standard light bulb was screwed, intended to relax and open the scalp's pores to stimulate hair growth [1]. Advertising claimed that hair roots were dormant rather than dead and that about 15 minutes a day of use would rejuvenate thinning hair, backed by a 30-day guarantee and customer testimonials.
No clinical studies of the Thermocap are known. Today it is used in histories of hair-loss remedies as an example of an early heat-and-light scalp device.
